characters: Mohammed: an energetic ten-year-old Ghanaian boy with short hair in a yellow shirt and khaki-brown school shorts.
Baah: his thoughtful ten-year-old Ghanaian male friend with short hair, slightly rounder cheeks, in a matching yellow shirt and khaki-brown school shorts.
Their teacher: a wise Ghanaian female Primary 4 teacher in a turquoise-and-leaf-green patterned dress, wearing rubber boots when working by the pond margin.

narrationPlan.voice: An eager boy’s voice for Mohammed; a thoughtful boy’s voice for Baah
narrationPlan.pace: Lively at first, then hushed, then bright (about 100 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A pond tune of frogs and crickets that fades, then returns (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Ponds, streams, wetlands, and sacred groves across Ghana sustain rich biodiversity. The story follows the NaCCA Basic 4 Science standard on ecosystems and interdependence (B4.3.3.1.1).

Highlights both ecological stewardship (wild-looking native plants provide vital habitat) and water safety (children never step into ponds or streams and only work on dry ground under adult supervision).

Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that ecological interdependence (shade, shelter, food, oxygen, and non-living factors) aligns with NaCCA B4.3.3.1.1.
Confirm water-margin safety is clearly modelled in both text and illustrations.

teacherGuide.overview: When two well-meaning pupils clear native plants from a school pond to make it look neat, they witness how habitat loss disrupts an ecosystem—and work with their teacher to restore its balance. Based on NaCCA Basic 4 Science.
learningGoals: Define an ecosystem as living things interacting with non-living surroundings.
Identify living components (plants, frogs, fish, insects) and non-living components (water, sunlight, air, soil).
Predict what happens when one component of an ecosystem is removed.
beforeReading: Ask: what living and non-living things can we spot in a school garden or under a shady tree?
whileReading: Pause on page 3 and let learners predict why the frogs and dragonflies disappeared.
afterReading: Play a “web of life” yarn game where each learner represents sun, water, soil, reed, insect, frog, or fish—then gently drop one strand to feel how others are affected.
Draw a local habitat and group its parts into Living and Non-Living.
discussion: Why can a natural habitat that looks “messy” to humans actually be healthy for wildlife?
Why should we always consult teachers or elders before altering a natural area?
reflection: Name one small habitat around your school or home that you can help protect.

support: Sort picture cards of a pond into two columns: Living Things and Non-Living Things.
stretch: Draw a four-step food chain for the pond starting with sunlight and green water plants.

culturalNotes: Ponds, streams, wetlands, and sacred groves across Ghana sustain rich biodiversity. The story follows the NaCCA Basic 4 Science standard on ecosystems and interdependence (B4.3.3.1.1).

Highlights both ecological stewardship (wild-looking native plants provide vital habitat) and water safety (children never step into ponds or streams and only work on dry ground under adult supervision).
localiseThis: Adapt the habitat example to a local garden, cocoa farm, grassland, lagoon, or forest edge.
Strict water safety: learners must never approach ponds, streams, or drains without adult supervision.

factCheck.claim: Aquatic plants regulate water temperature through shading, oxygenate water via photosynthesis, and provide food and shelter for invertebrates, fish, and amphibians within a pond ecosystem.
factCheck.explanation: Removing macrophytes increases solar heating, reduces dissolved oxygen refuge and cover, and disrupts pond trophic webs.
